locked_title: لماذا احتاجت كوريا الشمالية 187 لابتوب داخل بيوت أمريكية؟

claim_status_legend.CURRENT_ALLEGATION: Claim from a current indictment/complaint or law-enforcement action; not yet adjudicated.
claim_status_legend.PROVEN_CASE: Claim grounded in guilty plea, sentencing, conviction, or court-established facts from a prior related case.
claim_status_legend.AGENCY_OBSERVATION: Current FBI/agency threat observation; general pattern, not automatically attributable to every defendant in the current case.

claims.claim: On 2026-10-13 DOJ announced coordinated actions involving more than 70 U.S. companies and seizure of approximately 187 computer devices used in alleged DPRK remote-IT-worker schemes.
In Texas, the FBI searched more than 40 residences and seized a mix of laptops and KVM devices described as laptop-farm infrastructure.

In the Matthew Isaac Knoot case, employer laptops were shipped to his Nashville residences; unauthorized remote-desktop software let a North Korean IT worker operating from China appear to victim companies as if the worker were located in Nashville.

A separate multi-year scheme involving Kejia Wang and Zhenxing Wang used stolen identities, more than 100 U.S. companies and U.S.-hosted laptop farms, and generated more than $5 million in illicit revenue; both U.S. nationals were sentenced in 2026.

The FBI says DPRK IT workers increasingly use paid facilitators, remote-desktop software, KVM-over-IP devices, smaller distributed laptop farms, stolen identities and third-party freelancers to support fraudulent employment.

The FBI warns that once embedded, DPRK IT workers may create insider risk involving sensitive data theft and extortion; this is a general threat pattern and must not be presented as proven conduct by every person in the October 2026 action.
U.S.-based device hosting can help overseas workers circumvent controls that depend on the physical location of company-issued equipment.

In the Kejia Wang/Zhenxing Wang case, court-established facts described a multi-year scheme using stolen identities of more than 80 U.S. persons to obtain remote jobs at more than 100 U.S. companies. Kejia Wang supervised at least five U.S. facilitators who collectively hosted hundreds of victim-company computers at residences. The defendants also used shell companies and financial accounts to receive proceeds; DOJ said the scheme generated more than $5 million and facilitators collectively received nearly $700,000. Workers in the scheme gained access to sensitive employer data and source code, including ITAR-controlled data at a defense contractor.

The FBI's 2026 guidance says DPRK IT workers are increasingly using more facilitators, smaller distributed laptop farms with fewer laptops at each location, and third-party freelancers who may apply for jobs, conduct interviews, or perform portions or even entire jobs for a fraction of the salary.

title_accuracy_finding.finding: The locked title says 187 laptops, but the strongest current DOJ source describes approximately 187 computer devices, and the Texas source refers to laptops and KVM devices. The evidence does not cleanly support saying all 187 were laptops.
title_accuracy_finding.required_script_treatment: In the opening minute, explicitly state that the 187 figure refers to seized computer devices including laptops and KVM equipment, while the broader operation is commonly described as laptop-farm infrastructure.
